Android from the foundation · Puzzle 6 of 6

The main thread is one clerk with one queue

All UI and lifecycle code runs on one thread that handles messages from a queue, one at a time. A slow message blocks everything behind it.

The problem

The UI toolkit isn't thread-safe: if two threads changed the same view at once, it would break. And lifecycle messages from system_server arrive on Binder threads. So everything UI-related has to end up on one thread, in order.

See it

The building block

Inside your process:

  • MessageQueue: a list of messages ("run this"), sorted by when they should run.
  • Looper: an endless loop on one thread: take the next message, run it, repeat; sleep when the queue is empty.
  • Handler: the way to put a message into a particular Looper's queue.
val main = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())
main.post { textView.text = "Done" }        // runs when the clerk reaches it
main.postDelayed({ hideHint() }, 2_000)     // runs about 2 s later

Dispatchers.Main in coroutines is built on this same queue.

The analogy

One clerk at a desk with an in-tray. The clerk takes one letter at a time and finishes it before the next. Anyone, including the post office's couriers (Binder threads), can drop letters into the tray through the slot (a Handler).

Check yourself

onCreate() calls Thread.sleep(6000) and the user taps the screen. What happens?

The tap waits in the queue behind onCreate, isn't handled within 5 seconds, and the system shows an ANR.

What does handler.post { … } do?

It adds the code as a message to that Handler's Looper's queue, so that thread runs it when it gets there.

Why don't you need locks to update views?

Because only the main thread touches them, one message at a time.

Sources

  • Android Developers: Processes and threads overview
  • Android Developers: ANRs
  • Android reference: Handler
  • Android reference: Looper

What you now know

The full chain: system_server decides → Binder carries the message → a Binder thread posts it with a Handler → the main thread's Looper runs it → your callback. Keep every main-thread message short.
